talks.title: AI, AppSec, and You: A Practitioner's Diary
talks.teaser: Separates AI hype from practical gains in application security, using an MCP server for DefectDojo as the working example.
talks.summary:
The session asks whether AI will reshape application security the way cloud did, or whether it is an overheated bubble. The speaker, a DefectDojo co-founder, answers from his own experiments rather than predictions. He also raises the economics behind large AI vendors, including token costs, heavy data center spending and the risk that a few providers dominate the market.

The central case study is an MCP server built to expose DefectDojo findings to language models. The main lesson was that input quality matters more than the connector. Because DefectDojo already normalizes results from many scanners, the model receives one consistent view of a finding. Other practical points: send only the fields the model needs, since every token costs money; use result limits so a count query returns a single number; keep the server read-only; and treat tool descriptions as instructions the model will follow. The talk also covers running open-source models locally with Ollama and orchestration libraries such as LangChain, LangGraph and LangFlow. It explains how errors compound across multi-step agent chains, and how a DARPA entry placed deterministic checks between steps to keep accuracy up. Prompt injection, non-deterministic outputs and the lethal trifecta of untrusted input, sensitive data access and outbound communication are presented as design hazards.

The takeaways are to avoid tying a company to one AI vendor, to add guardrails and safety margins, to limit blast radius and to fail safely. The speaker closes with open problems he would like solved, such as linking findings to developer workflows and handling changing vendor output formats automatically.

talks.title: Out of Control: Promise Theory and the Future of Security Agents
talks.teaser: Frames security agents as autonomous nodes that make and keep explicit commitments, using a code review pipeline as a case study.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security teams are repeating an old habit by managing AI agents like guards or factory workers that wait for orders. The speaker warns that this approach yields brittle systems and misaligned incentives. In its place, the talk proposes Promise Theory, a model from Mark Burgess in which autonomous agents state what they will do, and trust grows as they keep or break those commitments over time.

Drawing on experience building an agentic code review product, the speaker described the problems that shaped the design: repeatable results, high accuracy, fast feedback, and limited visibility into the code around a change. The pipeline splits work among context-gathering, planning, verification, and exploitability agents, with specialized agents for each vulnerability class and models matched to each job. A benchmark across 26 vulnerabilities in four languages compared detection rates among several tools. An audience exercise had attendees name a security tool as an agent and list its promises and dependencies. The speaker also walked through the OWASP LLM Application Top 10, from prompt injection to unbounded consumption, and described a cost spike of roughly $2,500 caused by an agent searching a codebase without limits.

The closing point is that risk has become contextual, so analysis should weigh code intent, application design, and the operating environment rather than matching patterns alone. Practitioners should keep each agent's scope narrow, measure how reliably agents deliver on their commitments, and keep a developer in the loop for automated fixes.

talks.title: Navigating Challenges of Risk-Based Vul. Mgmt. in a Cloud World
talks.teaser: Explains how to prioritize vulnerabilities by business context, reachability and ownership across code, cloud and infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the problem: vulnerability volumes have grown into the hundreds of thousands, disclosure-to-exploitation windows have shrunk to days, and teams often juggle several scanners that each produce their own severity score. The speakers argue that spreadsheet-driven, severity-first triage leaves engineers frustrated and executives without shared context. They also note that asset ownership is often unclear, so findings reach the wrong team and stall.

The middle of the talk lays out a risk-based model. The presenters describe consolidating and deduplicating findings from different tools, then enriching them with exploit evidence, internet exposure and business criticality. They trace a vulnerability's lineage from source code through build files, artifacts, containers and registries, so the fix lands with the owner who can actually change it. Reachability analysis is used to set aside issues that cannot be triggered in the running environment. A funnel built from their own results shows the set of critical findings shrinking to a small fraction of the starting count.

The closing section frames the approach as collaboration between security, engineering and business sponsors. It suggests drawing ownership data from existing service catalogues rather than asking engineers to file tickets by hand. Practitioners should take away the idea of stewardship for assets, prioritizing by context rather than raw score, and measuring outcomes in time and effort saved. One of the presenters, speaking from a vendor position, also outlines product features for AI-assisted remediation.

talks.title: Invited Speaker
talks.teaser: Explains how cyber resilience, AI-driven attacks and software supply chain risk shape security priorities for organizations.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining cyber resilience as an organization's ability to keep operating during a cyber attack or a failed software integration. A hospital that loses its systems and must still admit patients serves as the example. The speaker links this to two 2024 events: a healthcare breach caused by missing multifactor authentication, and a worldwide outage triggered by a faulty security software update. Both pushed organizations to bring development, operations, legal and security teams together.

The middle section draws on survey data from her research at LevelBlue. It covers how AI makes phishing, voice calls and deepfake video more convincing, and how a group of young, English-speaking social engineers targeted help desks, UK retailers and a major car manufacturer. The data also shows that few organizations have a formal incident response plan or check cyber security during acquisitions, and that many have little visibility into their software suppliers, even though CEOs list the software supply chain among their top risks.

The closing section offers four steps: raise awareness of resilience, define what it means and who owns it, attach security metrics to every leader, and review third-party security practices on a regular schedule. In the question period, she advises reporting incidents to the board by business impact rather than every minor event, and says a codified response plan helps build the customer trust boards care about.

talks.title: AI from DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Explores how agentic AI will reshape DevSecOps pipelines, using metrics, adversary profiles and threat models as guides.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's view that AI gives security teams speed and scale, such as drafting a threat model in seconds that might otherwise take weeks. That time can go toward thinking about what attackers are actually doing. She traces how DevSecOps grew from small beginnings and argues that moving pipelines from automated, continuous checks to agent-driven ones will take a similar organic effort, with budgets and vendor roadmaps shifting along the way.

The middle section covers how to prepare. Agents tend to handle bounded problems and numeric goals better than loose wording, so she recommends starting with goal-oriented metrics, such as a "securability" score that rises when developers do well and falls when they do badly. Other building blocks include a capability map, a risk matrix, and an adversary scorecard that groups threats into profiles. Those profiles can trigger threat models, which in turn produce test cases and alerts that can be measured against adversary coverage. Human review stays in the loop, and several cooperating agents, coordinated by an orchestrator, are needed rather than one.

The closing portion turns to practical steps: mapping where agents fit, using prompts and shared tools to build these artifacts, and asking vendors for metric-driven reporting instead of relying only on questionnaires. The speaker concludes that the security job is changing rather than disappearing, and urges attendees to sharpen their prompting and choose a concrete next step.

talks.title: Is this the Most Dangerous Metric in Cybersecurity?
talks.teaser: Examines why percent-of-IT-spend cybersecurity benchmarks are unreliable and how leaders can budget without them.
talks.summary:
Justin Whitaker, a management consultant who advises CISOs on budgeting, opens with the pressure security leaders face when finance asks them to justify spending against peer benchmarks. He notes that published figures, such as a spread of roughly 4% to 17% of IT spend, are scarce, come from a handful of large consultancies, and rely on inconsistent methods. Unclear boundaries around what counts as security cost, such as identity management, developer time spent fixing findings, and awareness training, make comparisons unreliable.

He argues that the benchmarks also leave the important questions unanswered: whether higher spending measurably lowers risk, whether heavier spenders avoid breaches, and whether spending can ever level off as vendor costs rise and attackers adapt. Instead of anchoring to a percentage, he proposes a race-to-baseline approach. Maturity modeling, adapted from a Department of Energy framework, highlights weak domains and lets leaders set a target level tied to risk tolerance and a multi-year roadmap. In the Q&A he explained that the right figure depends on where an organization sits on that maturity curve, and that firms just starting out may need to roughly double their budgets.

For the business case, he recommends tying investment to specific capabilities rather than repeating the same regulatory and trust arguments each year. He also suggests building a bridge between security and finance staff so that costs and benefits are modeled more honestly. He closes by urging attendees to treat spending benchmarks with careful scrutiny.

talks.title: Open Source AI and Granite
talks.teaser: Explains why open AI models matter and walks through running and fine-tuning IBM's Granite model locally.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a complaint that many widely used AI models are closed: weights are distributed as opaque binaries, training data is hidden, and users face unclear legal exposure. The speaker, an IBM developer advocate, makes the case for openly documented models that outsiders can verify. He describes the Linux Foundation's AI governance work on defining what an open model is, and presents IBM's Granite family as an example, citing published training documentation and legal backing for customers.

The middle section explains fine-tuning compared with retrieval, using a library analogy to show when changing a model's knowledge is worth the cost at scale. He surveys agent frameworks and the sheer number of models on Hugging Face, then highlights smaller Granite variants built for narrow jobs, including one that can run on a Raspberry Pi. Real examples follow: triaging conference talk submissions by how much they read as sales pitches, a local tutor for medical interview practice, and generating bedtime stories paired with generated images. The live demo runs a time series model on a laptop CPU to forecast personal glucose and insulin readings.

The closing message is to pick a small local model for a specific job, keep a human reviewing outputs, and weigh licensing and data provenance when choosing a model. In the Q&A, the speaker noted that full training datasets are very large and rarely requested, and that the main limit for local use is GPU capacity.

talks.title: Hidden Risks of Integrating AI: Extracting Private Data with Real-World Exploits
talks.teaser: Shows how LLM, RAG and vector database features leak private data through repeated queries, embedding inversion and prompt injection.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a report stating that 13% of organizations had breaches involving their AI models or applications. The speaker argues that adding AI widens the attack surface in ways standard application security thinking does not cover, and that language models are probabilistic, so they cannot serve as a reliable security control. A short neural network demonstration shows how models learn from data and why their accuracy stops short of perfect.

The middle section focuses on extracting private data. A Llama model fine-tuned on synthetic personal records refused direct questions, but repeated queries eventually exposed a full record, including a passport number. Retrieval-augmented generation spreads copies of sensitive data into vector stores, prompts and logs. The speaker then showed that embeddings can be partly inverted with an inversion model, recovering names, dates and dollar amounts from a short message. Tool calls through model context protocol servers were also shown to leak an SSH key and note contents, driven by a malicious tool and hidden text in a note. Publicized incidents involving Microsoft Copilot and a calendar automation feature were cited as real-world examples.

The closing takeaways are to assume failure and guard against consequences, to mitigate data risks because AI systems multiply copies that are rarely monitored, and to trace every untrusted input to any action it can trigger. Practical steps include limiting automatic AI features, holding vendors to account on security, and encrypting data before storage, including vector encryption that resists inversion.

talks.title: The Cybersecurity-Minded Future, And How Security Champions Get Us There
talks.teaser: Shows how security champion programs bridge AppSec and engineering and drive lasting culture change.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing application security as a people problem. The speaker argues that human behavior remains the largest factor in organizational risk, and that AI-based tools will not remove the need for creative human defenders. He treats an AppSec program as a change program, using the diffusion of innovation model to explain why early adopters, or security champions, are needed to carry a message past the enthusiastic minority.

The middle of the talk turns to practice. He recommends building relationships across engineering first, then finding risk, fixing it, and only afterward investing in root-cause analysis and preventative controls. For measurement, he suggests tracking how often teams bring security in early, how thoroughly risk is covered, how quickly issues get fixed, and how much rework prevention saves, translated into cost. He also covers motivation through status, access, power and recognition, and lists common reasons programs fail, such as missing leadership buy-in, negative social proof, handing security work to champions, and running them without resources or fun.

He closes by stressing that culture change takes years, that programs must be tailored to the organization's own culture, and that recruiting new champions is continuous. Audience questions covered attrition, involving HR, and how to grow adoption beyond early adopters.

talks.title: The 6-Month AI Security Playbook for Startups
talks.teaser: Presents a six-month roadmap for startups to scale security with open-source and AI-assisted tools, without adding headcount.
talks.summary:
The talk frames security as a bottleneck for early-stage companies and argues that a lean startup can build a usable baseline within six months. The speaker uses a role-play in which a founding team must pass an investor's security due diligence, and suggests starting with vendor questions about data training, audits and AI guardrails, plus a simple tabletop exercise for an AI tool outage.

The middle covers a month-by-month plan. It starts with asset inventory using discovery tools such as Open-AudIT and Snipe-IT, then vulnerability scanning with OpenVAS, where an LLM condenses long reports into action steps. Detection follows, with Wazuh agents, dashboards, and n8n workflows that enrich indicators before alerting analysts. Incident response uses Shuffle playbooks alongside TheHive and Cortex for case handling. Compliance is handled with an open-source GRC suite that gathers evidence and flags gaps, and vendor risk is reviewed through document analysis and breach-data checks.

The closing advice is to track results such as mean time to respond, cases per analyst, and the share of vulnerabilities auto-remediated, so leadership can see the impact. The speaker stresses keeping human review on automated fixes and not sending confidential data to external AI services.

talks.title: Solving Secrets Sprawl Takes More Than Security: Why Machine Identity Is Everyone's Problem
talks.teaser: Shows why secrets sprawl needs cross-team ownership and maps a path toward short-lived, federated workload identity.
talks.summary:
Dwayne McDaniel opens by arguing that long-lived credentials, often called secrets sprawl, are among the largest risks organizations face, and that leaving the security team to take the blame after a breach misses the point. He describes non-human identities as the fast-growing majority of accounts in most enterprises and notes that credential abuse ranks as a leading root cause in recent breach reports. Drawing on public GitHub commit scanning, he reports that the share of repositories exposing a secret rose by about a quarter in each of the last two years, and that many leaked keys stay valid long after exposure.

The middle of the talk turns to ownership. McDaniel argues that responsibility for machine access is spread across security, developers, operations and executives, and that each group cares about different risks. He suggests framing the problem for executives and operations staff in terms of business risk and cost rather than fear. On the technical side, he walks through workload identity: services receive a verifiable identity at creation, exchange it for short-lived tokens, and so a leaked credential is worth little to an attacker. He points to recent Kubernetes features, SPIFFE and related IETF work, and secret managers as routes away from hard-coded keys.

The close offers a practical plan: inventory every credential, move secrets into a vault, use Git hooks to catch hard-coded values before they are committed, automate rotation, and make sure secrets can be revoked quickly during an incident. He stresses that this is a cross-team effort that needs budget and political will, and that security engineers should work inside developers' workflows rather than against them.

talks.title: When AI Goes Offensive, Exploiting the Unexploitable
talks.teaser: Demonstrates an AI agent that chains recon and misconfigurations into access-control exploits against web and cloud targets.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that manual reconnaissance and scanner-driven testing struggle with scale and depth, so the speaker's team has been building offensive AI agents that reason about a target the way a red teamer would. The agent design adds observe and judge steps to the usual reason-act-learn loop, so false positives get filtered before anyone spends hours chasing them. The stack described includes a model, a vector store that remembers past attempts, an agent framework and a crawler.

Two demonstrations follow. In the first, an agent starts from a token obtained with limited access in an assumed-breach scenario, reads its permissions, enumerates directory and application resources, and plans a multi-stage chain that ends with persistent backdoor accounts in a Microsoft Graph environment. When a step fails, the error is passed to another agent that revises the approach. In the second, a single agent works through an unauthenticated file-read flaw in a Kafka Connect deployment, creating a malicious connector and confirming access to sensitive system files.

The takeaways are practical. Agents need a defined role, a narrow scope and explicit safety constraints in their prompts, and a human should steer them early. Model choice and token cost shape results, and the speaker sees the most value in recon and in carrying context forward between steps.

talks.title: DevSecOps as a Launchpad
talks.teaser: Explores how embedding security into AI-assisted coding and MCP-connected tools can reduce friction in DevSecOps pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing security as a source of friction in fast delivery cycles, especially as AI-assisted coding speeds up feature work. The speakers trace the shift-left idea from its origins toward checks throughout the lifecycle, then walk through the DevSecOps toolchain: static analysis that inspects source code, dynamic testing that probes a running application, and dependency analysis that checks third-party components against vulnerability databases. They point to fragmented tooling, false positives and slow feedback as recurring pain points that push developers away from security processes.

The middle section surveys recent AI and data regulation, including a US executive order, the EU AI Act, DORA, India's privacy law and the NIST AI risk management framework. It then turns to AI-generated code, where training data, outdated dependencies and non-deterministic output can introduce weaknesses. The speakers explain the Model Context Protocol as a way to give models structured, controlled access to tools and data, and outline the host, client and server roles along with local and remote server deployment.

The closing vision is to connect scanners to MCP servers so the coding assistant runs SAST and SCA while code is being written, letting many findings be fixed before commit and reducing pipeline iterations. In audience questions, the speakers acknowledged that MCP servers carry their own risks, that data exposure must be managed, and that scanner latency inside the IDE is an open concern. The takeaway is to make security tooling seamless for developers while governing which servers and tools are trusted.

talks.title: [SPOILERS] 20 Minutes into the MCP future
talks.teaser: Gives API developers a quick overview of the Model Context Protocol, its architecture, and its security risks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a problem: APIs were built for humans who read documentation and experiment, while AI agents need to discover tools, authentication and parameters on their own. The speaker uses a short example of a language model failing to answer a question about recent events to show why models need access to outside context, then compares the tool-calling schemas used by different model vendors, which each describe functions differently.

The middle section introduces the Model Context Protocol as an open, JSON-RPC based standard first published in late 2024. It explains the three roles in the design: a host such as a desktop assistant or code editor, a client that the host creates for each server, and a server that exposes tools and their parameters. The talk covers local transport over standard input and output, remote transport over HTTP, and how a model can query several servers in turn to gather context. Recent additions such as remote servers and OAuth are noted, along with a registry for finding servers and a brief mention of agent-to-agent protocols.

The closing part focuses on security. Examples include directory traversal through unchecked file paths, command injection caused by concatenating shell strings, wrapping a whole API as one tool that can trigger destructive actions, and prompt injection hidden in documents or tool descriptions. The speaker's advice is to separate read and write permissions, keep the blast radius small, require human approval for actions that cannot be reversed, and apply existing API security guidance until MCP-specific guidance matures.

talks.title: The Model Context Protocol: Convenience meets vulnerability
talks.teaser: Maps the Model Context Protocol's attack surface, including tool poisoning, rug pulls and authorization flaws, with defensive measures.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Model Context Protocol, which lets AI clients connect to external tools, data resources and prompt templates through MCP servers. The speaker walks through the client-server handshake, the tool listing and tool call flow, and the server-to-client features of sampling, elicitation and logging, explaining why these connections widen what an AI assistant can reach.

The middle section covers three areas of risk. Tool poisoning hides malicious instructions in tool descriptions that the model reads but users do not see, and the speaker cites tests in which clients followed such hidden directions without asking for approval. Authorization problems arise when an MCP server acts as both resource server and authorization server under the earlier specification, which fragments discovery endpoints and complicates enterprise identity integration. Rug pulls occur when a tool that was approved later changes its description or behavior silently. The speaker notes that new MCP issues appear so frequently that a complete catalogue was impractical.

The closing part gives practical advice: treat untrusted servers with caution, review tool descriptions before they reach the model, scan and sanitise descriptions, apply trust on first use with alerts on change, disable unused servers, and keep a human approving sensitive actions. The speaker proposes separating the identity provider from MCP resource servers, and invites the community to help build a deliberately vulnerable MCP test project.

talks.title: When the Tool is the Weapon Abusing (and defending) native M365 applications
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers abuse Teams, SharePoint and OneNote in business email compromise, and how to harden them.
talks.summary:
Alexis Watters, an email forensic investigator who handles business email compromise cases mostly for small and mid-sized businesses, opens by arguing that attackers now look well beyond the mailbox. Her caseload has grown quickly, the time from a phishing email to a compromised account has shrunk to minutes, and multi-factor authentication is often bypassed through reverse proxies and phishing kits, so layered defenses matter more than any single control.

The middle of the talk covers abuse of Microsoft 365 applications outside email. Attackers have messaged users in Teams posing as recruiters or help desk staff, then used calls to obtain credentials or MFA codes. Shared SharePoint and OneNote links set to anyone-with-the-link or anonymous access let attackers pull files and spread lures from a compromised tenant. Power BI pages have served as intermediate hops in phishing chains, and compromised global admins have added inbound connectors to push spam that carries Microsoft IP addresses. Attackers have also browsed Teams chats to locate files quickly and used Viva Insights to see whether their lures were opened.

The closing section gives defenders practical steps. Restrict Teams external access to trusted domains, tighten SharePoint sharing and anonymous access, separate admin accounts from daily mailboxes, and confirm the unified audit log is enabled, since it is the main source for investigations. She also stresses a culture where staff report suspicious clicks early rather than being blamed, and expects Copilot and AI summaries to be abused next.

talks.title: AI-Powered Security: Strengthening Cloud-Native Apps Against Emerging Threats
talks.teaser: Surveys how AI tools strengthen cloud-native DevSecOps and runtime defense, and how attacks like prompt injection threaten AI systems.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem facing security teams running cloud-native systems: microservices, containers and serverless functions produce far more logs, metrics and traces than people can review, and attacks can unfold faster than manual response. The speaker argues that AI can cut noise in code scanning, for instance by checking whether a flagged vulnerability is reachable and by proposing fixes as automated pull requests. Infrastructure-as-code review can catch risky combinations of settings that simple linters miss, while runtime tools learn normal behaviour and flag deviations.

The middle section turns to attacks on AI systems. It covers adversarial examples, data poisoning, model extraction and inversion, and prompt injection, both direct and indirect, including hidden instructions planted in documents or emails that assistants process. Supply chain risks in model hubs and ML libraries such as TensorFlow and PyTorch are also covered, including malicious pickled models.

The closing part walks through a hypothetical customer support chatbot on Kubernetes, mapping controls to each stage from development through build and deployment. The speaker proposes a six-layer defence covering secure ML pipelines, input and output validation, continuous monitoring, red teaming, zero trust and automated incident response. Practical takeaways include inventorying AI systems, testing against the OWASP LLM Top 10, signing models, maintaining an ML bill of materials and setting up AI governance.

talks.title: Fixing My Fixing Talk: What We Got Wrong (and Right) About AI Auto-Remediation
talks.teaser: Shows how a prompt-driven pipeline filters false positives and generates verifiable code fixes, and where AI remediation still fails.
talks.summary:
Eitan Worcel revisits a talk from the previous year, where he argued that AI could not reliably fix code vulnerabilities. Six months of research at his company, Mobb, led him to a more nuanced view. He starts by noting how widely AI-generated code is now in use, and argues that tools should help fix the flaws it introduces. The central concern is reliability, since developers stop trusting tools that give inconsistent or inaccurate changes.

The core of the talk is a blueprint for generating fixes. Per-vulnerability prompts are built from public guidance and large collections of real vulnerable code. A first prompt separates true positives from false positives, with reasoning attached, so fixes are only generated for real issues. Fix prompts are then refined through repeated test runs and human review, with a second model used to critique them. Worcel shows a fix that looked correct but only partly sanitized input, and describes other failures, such as deleted file content and a removed return statement. Early prompts succeeded only 10 to 15 percent of the time, improving to roughly 70 to 90 percent after iteration.

He closes with practical lessons: validate every fix with syntax and style checks, keep changes minimal, use deterministic code for simple patterns to control cost, and keep a human in the loop. Accuracy matters more than coverage, and knowing when a tool fails matters most.

talks.title: AI Beyond the Sales Pitch: A Project Manager's Experience
talks.teaser: Explains how a project manager's AI deployments in regulated sectors reveal red and green flags around data, outputs and explainability.
talks.summary:
Curtis, a senior project manager working across several sectors, opens by separating narrow AI, which performs one defined task, from the broader and agentic systems often promised in sales pitches. She contrasts automation, which repeats fixed steps, with AI that recognises patterns, and explains that pattern matching is not the same as reasoning. Her central framework is a three-part check: the data source, the desired output, and explainability, meaning the ability to trace how an answer was produced.

Through case studies and audience exercises, she applies that framework to real projects. An insurance first-notice-of-loss pilot showed why emotionally sensitive calls should stay with people. A lottery rules assistant succeeded after a phased rollout, first to internal testers and then to call-centre staff. A celebrity chat project stalled on the cost of a premium model used for long conversations. A university enrollment tool surfaced translation and access-control problems, while an HR assistant worked well once it lived inside Slack, where staff already were.

She closes with practical advice. When an answer looks wrong, trace it back to its source document, since outdated content is a common cause. Do not default to the most expensive model; switching to a cheaper one after tuning saved budget in one inventory project. Define an acceptable answer rather than a perfect one, bring in content, developer and in-between experts, and expect testing to stall when knowledge stays within the original team.

talks.title: Under the Radar: How we found 0-days in the Build Pipeline of OSS Packages
talks.teaser: Shows how CI/CD workflows in open source projects leak secrets and can be hijacked through pull requests.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the claim that build pipelines in open source projects are an underexamined part of the software supply chain. CI/CD systems run with high privileges, hold secrets such as publishing tokens and signing keys, and react to events from outside contributors, which makes them attractive targets. The speaker walks through recent incidents in which a popular GitHub Action and an npm release workflow were abused, leading to exposed credentials and malicious package versions, and notes that an AI coding agent helped introduce one of the vulnerable workflows.

The middle of the talk covers the main vulnerability classes. Dangerous triggers such as pull_request_target can expose secrets to pull requests from forks. Template injection occurs when untrusted fields such as issue bodies or branch names are interpolated into scripts. Bots such as Dependabot can be abused as a confused deputy, and non-ephemeral self-hosted runners allow persistence. The speaker introduces the idea of "living off the pipeline", where legitimate tools such as static site generators, scanners and shells are steered into running attacker code through config files or environment variables. A live demo walks through progressively harder exploits against a practice repository. The team also reports scanning around 200,000 repositories, with a large number of workflow findings and many disclosures to affected maintainers.

The closing guidance is practical. Teams should restrict which actions can run, default workflow tokens to read-only, require approval for workflows triggered by outside contributors, use protected environments and OIDC instead of long-lived credentials, pin dependencies, and avoid self-hosted runners in public repositories. Static analysis of workflow files and runtime monitoring of runners are suggested as additional layers.

talks.title: LLMs in AppSec: Why They Still Need a Chaperone
talks.teaser: Shows why LLMs need deterministic tooling, data preparation and human oversight to be useful for application security.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by contrasting large language models' success in areas like content drafting, translation and data analysis with their weaker fit for application security. AppSec demands exact, reproducible results, clear evidence for sign-off, awareness of a constantly changing threat landscape, and an understanding of how a system behaves at runtime. Mistakes can carry severe consequences, so prompting alone is not enough to meet that bar.

Using concrete examples, the speaker shows how a model reasoning over static inputs such as architecture diagrams and configuration files can miss services that open random ports at runtime, unless live scanner output is fed into it. The talk covers package hallucination, where models suggest dependencies that do not exist and attackers can register them. It also describes an experiment in which a model was asked to write static analysis rules and to build exploits that confirm or rule out findings. The model often produced fake proofs, and it struggled with confident, small incremental edits that repeatedly failed to build.

The practical takeaways are to break the work into small modules, give each component only the tools it needs, state requirements explicitly, and rely on deterministic tools and careful data preparation. Supervisor agents, output templates and frequent quality checks help keep results consistent, and humans should stay involved at chosen decision points. The talk closes by framing the goal as building and testing a working system around the model rather than trusting the model on its own.

talks.title: Bridging the Chasm: Filling the Security Knowledge Gap between Academia and Industry
talks.teaser: Explains why computer science programs leave graduates without security skills and what schools and employers can do.
talks.summary:
Mike Biocchi opens with a gap he saw while teaching computer science in Canada and the United States. Many graduates finish four-year degrees without taking a security course, and students in his classes could not explain basics such as hashing versus encryption, how HTTPS works, or the CIA triad. Using a student email and his experience updating an outdated fourth-year course, he frames the problem as a mismatch between what schools teach and what employers expect.

The middle of the talk walks through figures he gathered from university and college curriculum pages. Security courses are common as electives but much less often required for graduation. Industry surveys from 2022 and 2024 show many organizations still struggling to find staff with the skills they need. He also describes how slowly curricula change, sometimes taking around two years to update a course, and how developers under delivery pressure treat security findings as added cognitive load. That problem grows as AI-generated code reaches production, often without reviewers who recognize insecure patterns.

He closes with partial remedies: closer ties between academia and industry through advisory boards and co-op placements, partnerships with certification bodies, and a dedicated required security course that covers ethics and privacy alongside technical material. The takeaway for educators and employers is to treat basic secure coding knowledge as a baseline rather than a specialty, and to make small curriculum changes that can happen now.

talks.title: Builders & Breakers: A Collab Look at Securing LLM-Integrated Apps
talks.teaser: Pairs a builder and a penetration tester to show LLM prompt injection attacks alongside layered defenses for AI-integrated apps.
talks.summary:
The session pairs an application builder with a penetration tester who specialises in AI red teaming. It starts by contrasting traditional software with LLM-integrated applications, where the infrastructure looks much the same but meaning now matters as well as syntax. Two entries from the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, prompt injection and data poisoning, frame the rest of the talk.

The offensive part uses a demo of a refund chatbot for a web shop, where a model decides whether refunds are granted. Simple rewording and fake formatting can flip the decision, and a poisoned training example can force approvals. The tester also fuzzes the chatbot's endpoint with thousands of injection payloads through a Burp extension, and some nonsense answers get accepted. Bug bounty data shows vendors downgrading jailbreaks and prompt leaks, so researchers are pushed toward issues with real impact such as data access.

The defensive part covers moderation services, classifiers and open-source AI firewalls, which can still be bypassed, along with trust boundaries and access control on the functions a model can call. A GitLab chatbot case shows how a planted comment led to private code leaking through rendered HTML and an image request; a strict content security policy and sanitised output would have blocked it. The takeaways: classic appsec controls still apply, testing must be repeated because outputs vary and models change, and the application builder shares responsibility for defences.

talks.title: Technology and Leadership in Complex Times: Empowering Women in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Examines barriers women face in cybersecurity careers and offers practical ways to build pipelines and leadership paths.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's own career path, from years as a lead software developer into product security. He had to learn exploitation and risk concepts largely from scratch after the move, and he describes how his goal of managing a team stayed constant despite the change of field. He frames the session around the underrepresentation of women in a field that remains male-dominated.

The session then became an open discussion among attendees. Participants described being called too aggressive or bossy for behavior that is accepted in men, being asked about childcare instead of being offered growth opportunities, and having their ideas interrupted or credited to others. Several noted that these small slights accumulate and push capable people to plateau. Other points included a cited survey showing a steep drop in women's share of roles from manager to director, job descriptions that deter applicants who do not meet every listed requirement, and a salary negotiation where a female candidate was offered less than the budget allowed.

The practical guidance covered both organizations and individuals. Organizations were urged to sponsor women, give stretch assignments, provide leadership training, offer flexible work, run confidential reporting channels, and write neutral job descriptions. Individuals were encouraged to negotiate pay and benefits, build mentor networks through local and online communities, and describe their work with functional job titles. The speaker closed by urging attendees to speak up, act and support others.

talks.title: The Dark Side of AI: Developing unsecure applications in minutes
talks.teaser: Shows how AI-generated .NET and React code can ship with injection, XSS and authentication flaws, and how to catch them.
talks.summary:
Chris Lindsey, a field CTO with a background in healthcare software and security program leadership, opens by explaining why AI-assisted development matters and how quickly developers have adopted it. He walks through common prompting patterns, such as asking for a basic .NET Core CRUD application with Entity Framework and SQL Server, and argues that more specific prompts and breaking work into smaller steps produce better output.

The live build covers a backend and a React frontend generated mainly with Claude, with ChatGPT and Copilot also tried. Each model produced code that looked plausible, and when asked to secure it, the assistant added authentication, JWT handling, validation and rate limiting. The review then exposed gaps: a database connection string kept in configuration rather than a secrets manager, a password policy that differed between frontend and backend, an outdated serialization library with known risk, a CDN script loaded without a correct integrity hash, and encoding applied in the wrong layer. Compared with enterprise scanners, the assistants missed issues such as path traversal, log injection and regular expression denial of service.

The takeaways are to treat AI output as a draft from a developer without security training, to review diffs and run scanners before anything reaches production, to keep guardrails and coding standards in files the model can reference, to avoid pulling external dependencies live, and to rely on parameterized queries rather than generated sanitization.

talks.title: Why LLMs Fall Short in Vulnerability Management
talks.teaser: Tests LLMs on CVE detection, false positives, patch validation and malicious commit spotting, and reports where they fall short.
talks.summary:
Itamar Sher, who has spent about fifteen years in vulnerability research, opens by challenging vendor claims that LLMs can take over vulnerability management. He starts with a review of existing research, which suggests models handle short, simple bugs reasonably well but struggle as scope grows, with weak grasp of program flow and logical errors. He then describes four small experiments: identifying CVEs in single-file C code, measuring false positives on patched code, generating and judging security patches, and flagging malicious commits in JavaScript dependencies.

The results were mostly discouraging. Correct weakness classification and correct function identification were both low, and the model often misread the vulnerability entirely. Leading prompt wording pushed false positives from about 45 to 55 percent. An LLM used as a patch judge was wrong about 40 percent of the time, so manual review was still required. The commit scanner caught all twelve real-world malicious commits in its test set, but it also flagged poor coding practices and remained exposed to prompt injection.

The closing advice is to keep prompts neutral and concise, supply relevant context but not unrelated code, run models repeatedly because outputs vary, and keep a human in the loop. The speaker found LLMs most useful for suggesting patches, assisting with backports, and building in-house commit review tooling, rather than trusting them to triage findings unattended.

talks.title: Hacking a backup power solution(s) for your home, Tornado tested!
talks.teaser: Shows how a layered home backup power setup held up through a tornado and a multi-day grid outage, and where it failed.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a home backup power setup performed when an F2 tornado hit near Temple, Texas, in May 2024 and left the area without grid power for several days. The speaker, an incident responder, had built a layered system before the storm. It combined supplemental solar panels, a solar-capable mini-split air conditioner for a cool office, portable battery stations, a dual-fuel generator connected through a generator inlet, and a solar tracker. He describes the outage timeline and what he had to respond to as things went wrong.

Several parts of the setup held up well. A solar tracker survived the high winds because it lay flat, and the solar mini-split kept an office comfortable. Other parts failed or needed changes. Early on, the generator ran only briefly on small propane cylinders, and fuel for it was hard to find. A battery station's low charge limit had not been raised before storms arrived. The gasoline generator would not start until a battery charger powered from the solar system jump-started it. Open-frame generator output tripped UPS units and upset some electronics. Siphoning fuel from modern cars also proved impractical. A damaged aluminum lug at the meter base caused a fault once power returned, and the utility had to replace the meter.

The practical takeaways are to test the full backup chain before you need it, keep fuel and propane stocked, and use inverter generators with clean sine-wave output for sensitive electronics. The speaker also recommends writing a runbook so other household members can start and operate the system. The talk is a practitioner's account of applying disaster recovery to home power.

talks.title: Conquering Vulnerabilities: Human-Led, AI-Supported Code Surveillance
talks.teaser: Shows how a human reviewer can pair with an AI tool to run staged secure code reviews and keep them current.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI helps secure code review only when a human stays in charge of every step. Reading code is a distinct skill, and reviews are often squeezed or skipped. Instead of line-by-line reading, the approach concentrates on the parts of an application that hold the most valuable assets, tracing data flows toward them. AI speeds up summarising and triage, while people supply intent, business logic judgment and common sense.

The middle of the talk covers a staged workflow packaged as a Claude skill: business context, assets, attack surface, data flows, then a report. A reviewer checks each stage before it feeds the next, because early hallucinations would otherwise propagate. In a live demo on an older personal project, the tool flagged an unauthenticated MCP server over SSE as the most critical issue and produced a report with fifteen findings the speaker judged valid. The run took hours and many tokens, and the tooling was described as alpha quality.

To close, the talk proposes re-running the pipeline on each push, restarting from whichever stage a change affects and having a human review only the deltas. The core trade-off is speed versus coverage, and false positives can quickly erode trust with developers. AI should be treated as an assistant, not an authority.

talks.title: Death By (Python) Pickle: "Betrayal ML"
talks.teaser: Shows how Python pickle files can hide executable code inside machine learning models shared on public hubs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a light analogy: a machine learning model is a set of learned behaviors that can be loaded into another system, much like uploading a skill. It explains that a pickle file is Python's serialization format for packaging such data, and that the danger starts when a file meant to hold only data also carries instructions that run on load. The speaker points to public model hubs, which host large numbers of these files, and notes that many are too big for common sandboxes to analyze fully.

The middle of the talk walks through examples of pickle files found to create processes, reach the network, download a backdoor and run it. The speaker contrasts this with supply chain attacks on software releases, where a single partially signed package carried malware. He argues that a scanner reporting "no malware found" may only mean the file was too large or in an unsupported format, and that hash and reputation checks miss new threats. He describes watching for behavioral changes across releases, such as newly added checks for virtual machines, as a way to spot tampering, and mentions software bills of materials and emerging AI bills of materials as ways to inventory components.

The closing section returns to the basic question of what a pickle file is and reinforces that a model file should contain only data. The practical takeaways are to treat model files as untrusted code, to look beyond hashes and reputation when analyzing them, to keep inventories of AI components, and to monitor how software behaves from one release to the next.

talks.title: Improving Account Security with ITDR
talks.teaser: Shows how identity threat detection and response spots account takeover and fraud from authentication event logs.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works on identity products, argues that generic detection creates noise. Simple rules, such as flagging impossible travel from IP geolocation alone, can fire on VPN users or relay addresses, which leads to alert fatigue and missed signals. The talk makes the case for account-centric detection that builds context around each identity and accounts for the business setting, since staff, students and truck drivers each behave differently.

Identity threat detection and response (ITDR) platforms ingest application logs, enrich events with signals such as hosting provider, VPN status, breached email, obsolete user agents and phone number type, and combine them into risk scores. Real examples include impossible travel, a credential stuffing campaign with millions of attempts over two days that led to some account takeovers, and session tokens shared to reach the same application from other places. Complementary methods include browser device fingerprinting, honeypots and canary keys. Observations from millions of daily events, such as rising IPv6 traffic, bot-like user agents that turned out to come from iOS message previews, and homoglyph lookalike domains, show how easily rules can mislead.

The closing advice is to measure how quickly a tool detects each attack type, since a week of delay gives attackers ample room, and to confirm that it can scale. Tuning should reduce friction for legitimate users, with step-up authentication used sparingly and automated responses added once rules mature. Analysts should feed exceptions back into the system so they are not overwhelmed by individual events.

talks.title: Using Agentic Systems to Revolutionize Static Analysis
talks.teaser: Shows how agentic AI can find source code vulnerabilities without the parsers and hand-written rules that traditional static analysis needs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the limits of conventional static analysis. Building a checker means parsing each language, generating call graphs, and writing source, sink and passthrough models for every language version, framework and package. Any gap in that coverage becomes a missed vulnerability, and results are largely yes-or-no, so business logic and configuration flaws are hard to express as rules.

The speakers then describe Project Pigeon, an internal agentic system that works on raw source text instead of syntax trees or call graphs. It splits the analysis into small units of work, with guardrails and oversight agents that validate each stage's inputs and outputs. Their first attempt, a single supervisor agent given a whole codebase, skipped most files and reported work it had not done, which pushed them toward a staged, programmatically controlled design. They showed findings in real open source projects that led to maintainer fixes, and a SQL injection in pseudo-code that the system flagged without knowing the language. They also described supply chain incidents where individually minor suspicious behaviours were chained into a more serious picture.

The closing section covered cost, scan time and non-determinism. One Rust codebase of about 4,500 lines cost roughly four dollars and took 11 minutes, and repeated scans can add or drop single findings. The speakers argued that the system should be judged like a human code reviewer rather than a scanner, and that it works best on focused, security-sensitive code. They use off-the-shelf models chosen per task rather than fine-tuned ones. Their takeaway is that AI should augment traditional static analysis, and that the surrounding framework matters more than the model itself.

talks.title: Taming the Twin Red Hat Beasts: A Compliance Gladiator's Epic Tale
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a CIS hardening baseline for RHEL 8 and 9 and group scan results without costly commercial tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk covers building a secure configuration baseline for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and 9 in an environment where most administrators work with Windows tooling. The speaker frames the problem: CIS benchmarks contain hundreds of line items, vendors ship default builds that favor getting things to work, and a documented baseline is often treated as a box to tick. He argues that the baseline should be a policy-level document, with each item marked as accepted, defined differently, or rejected, backed by a justification and a plan of action for the remaining gaps.

The middle of the talk turns to scanning. Commercial scanner output was described as hard to act on, with results passing or failing in different forms across a server population. The approach shown was to pull raw results from every host, group them by benchmark ID and by identical output, and load the groups into a spreadsheet. Servers that share a result cluster together, which makes outliers and inconsistent configurations visible quickly. The speaker also described parsing messy CSV and XML exports with custom code, and comparing benchmark versions where numbering and wording had changed between releases.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to start in non-production, change one thing at a time, record legacy exceptions as documented deviations, and validate that settings are actually applied on every system. AI tools can help triage generic guidance, but business context and application needs still drive the final decisions. The method is presented as a practical path rather than a finished product, with formal audit validation still pending when the talk was given.

talks.title: Why so serious? Making Incident Response More Effective With a Curiosity Mindset
talks.teaser: Argues that curiosity, rather than more tooling, can make overloaded incident response teams more effective with what they already have.
talks.summary:
Sarah Fuller opens by defining incident response as contextualizing, validating and acting on alerts and requests that demand critical thinking. She argues that automation and formal training take time many teams lack, so a culture of curiosity can help sooner. In her framing, curiosity means asking questions, seeking peer input, owning what you learn and aligning work with business priorities.

The middle of the talk compares the NIST incident response lifecycle with the SANS DARE model. Fuller rewrites each stage as a question an analyst should answer, such as whether an alert reflects real intent to harm. She contrasts passive habits, like waiting for alerts or accepting an automated verdict, with active ones like baselining behavior and hunting for unknowns. Her main case involved a web application firewall alert that repeatedly auto-blocked accounts. By building a 90-day baseline and contacting the identity team, she found the account owners, which led to alert tuning and a lasting cross-team relationship. A second example describes a tool inventory she built during onboarding, which an engineering team later needed and which grew through a team exercise.

In closing, she answers audience questions about building rapport with remote colleagues, handling discouraged curiosity and avoiding burnout. Her practical advice is to build relationships across teams, leave yourself notes for low-energy days and aim for consistent delivery.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Certifications, Career Planning, and Current AI Impact
talks.teaser: Explains how to pick among hundreds of cybersecurity certifications and build a career plan around them.
talks.summary:
Dean Bushmiller opens by contrasting the field when he started, with three security certifications, against today's several hundred. He argues that this volume makes choosing hard, and he frames certification as one part of a longer career plan rather than a one-off purchase. The session is interactive, with audience polls on interests and experience and questions taken throughout.

The middle section covers what he considers credible credentials. He is skeptical of exams sold bundled with mandatory training, tests without a published outline, unproctored exams, and study material built on leaked questions. He prefers vendor-neutral certifications and uses the NICCS workforce framework to map careers to the knowledge, skills and abilities each role requires. He recommends gathering feedback from many people rather than one or two, and building skill through deliberate practice and structured reading.

He closes with practical steps: write a short plan, start with a small certification to build momentum, then commit to a larger one for the long term. He suggests staying in your current industry where possible and using unusual activities such as beta testing to stand out in interviews. On AI credentials, he expects vendor-specific offerings to mature first and says vendor-neutral AI security certifications are not yet trustworthy, with a likely wait of several years.

talks.title: Security Considerations for Copilot for Microsoft 365
talks.teaser: Explains how Copilot for Microsoft 365 respects permissions and labels, and which safeguards organizations should configure first.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a Microsoft 365 consultant, starts by arguing that comparing Copilot with general chatbots misses the point. Its value comes from working inside Word, Excel, Teams, Outlook and SharePoint. The core risk he describes is that Copilot can reach whatever the signed-in user can open, so overshared files, stale permissions and ad hoc grants become the real exposure.

The middle of the session walks through a set of controls. These include a sensitivity label taxonomy, automatic labeling for sensitive data types, DLP rules that stop Copilot from processing labeled content, watermarking, alerting and conditional access tied to device and location. In a live demo, a label that withheld the extract permission made Copilot refuse to summarize a document, and a DLP policy enforced that restriction. He also covered retention, communication compliance, insider risk management, guest reviews, quarterly permission reviews and the fact that some controls depend on license tier.

He closes with practical advice. Start with the business problem, train users so they adopt the tool, and roll out protections in phases, beginning with MFA and classification. He pointed to DSPM for AI in Purview for reviewing which AI apps touch sensitive data, and to the Defender portal for alerts.

talks.title: Navigating the AI Minefield: Threat Modeling for Emerging AI Risks
talks.teaser: Walks through threat modeling AI systems with STRIDE and MAESTRO, covering prompt injection, data poisoning and model inversion.
talks.summary:
Threat modeling for AI systems needs more than a standard checklist, because model outputs are less predictable and the risks reach beyond security into fairness and user trust. The talk opens by arguing that core principles such as authentication, least privilege, input validation, logging and monitoring still hold for AI. It then shows how STRIDE can be applied to AI components like data pipelines, models and APIs, using examples such as spoofing a fake model or tampering with training data.

The middle section surveys AI-specific threats: training data poisoning, model inversion, direct and indirect prompt injection, insecure output handling and overreliance on AI decisions. For each, the speaker pairs the attack with mitigations such as trusted data sources, access gating, output filtering, hardened instruction sets, sandboxed tool execution and human approval for critical actions. Resources from OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, NIST and Google's secure AI framework are mentioned, along with MAESTRO for multi-agent setups.

The closing case study applies this to a fictional banking assistant that feeds user feedback into training data and calls external APIs. The speaker identifies critical assets and trust zones, then maps threats and controls onto them. The main takeaway is that threat modeling should happen at design time, be revisited iteratively, and guide testing so the highest-priority threats are validated.

talks.title: How AI is perceived in shift left of Appsec
talks.teaser: Examines how AI could change application security work, from threat modeling and code review to DAST and pentesting.
talks.summary:
Anitha Dakamarri, a longtime application security practitioner, opens by describing how AppSec teams work alongside developers across the software development lifecycle, from architecture reviews and threat modeling through code review, dynamic testing and penetration tests. She argues that generative and agentic AI will bring new strains: AppSec teams will need skills for AI systems, and they will need to coordinate with data science, legal and privacy groups, since AI output is non-deterministic and models change over time.

Mid-talk, she covers where AI could help. Threat modeling could be automated by reviewing design documents and suggesting attack scenarios that include data poisoning and prompt injection. AI-assisted static analysis could reduce duplicate and false-positive findings and offer context-specific fixes, and it could prioritize issues by severity and impact. For DAST, she describes context-aware crawling to find hidden APIs that scanners miss, and for pentesting she highlights attack-path analysis that follows an initial exploit through lateral movement. The discussion also covers software bills of materials and the gap between listing a library and knowing whether a vulnerable function is reachable, with VEX suggested as one way to close it.

She closes by framing the shift as safety left, where ethical and AI-specific risks join security concerns early in development. Her takeaways are that AI can improve developer experience through faster feedback, and that the field faces a shortage of engineers skilled in testing generative AI applications.

talks.title: Curating Secure Software: The Art of Selecting Safe Dependencies
talks.teaser: Walks developers through evaluating open source dependencies for security, licensing, tampering and maintenance risk before adoption.
talks.summary:
The talk treats software curation as the careful selection and upkeep of third-party dependencies, much as a museum vets what it displays. It opens with a recent case in which a widely used npm package was hijacked after its maintainer's account was taken over through an email-based two-factor reset. The speaker notes that most application code comes from external suppliers, often maintained by a small number of people, so a single compromise can reach many downstream applications.

The speaker argues that known vulnerabilities are only one risk to weigh. Other concerns include leaked secrets, license conflicts, such as a router vendor forced to release its source code, tampered or unsigned packages, and deep transitive dependencies that teams rarely see. Using a tangled string of holiday lights as a metaphor for a dependency tree, she explains how CVE, CVSS and CISA's KEV catalog differ, and how SBOM formats such as CycloneDX and SPDX help locate components. She also cites the short window, reportedly around 15 minutes, in which attackers begin scanning after a vulnerability is announced.

Her takeaways are practical. Before adopting a package, check its maintainer count, project health, community responsiveness and security practices. Keep an inventory of third-party components, scan regularly with free tools, and upgrade on a defined cadence, usually one or two versions behind the newest release rather than always adopting the latest. She also suggests a registry proxy that delays newly published versions.

talks.title: Small TPM with a Power of Big HSM
talks.teaser: Explains how TPM 2.0 can protect cryptographic keys in medical devices, using Linux key hierarchies and access controls.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how hardware-backed encryption has been used in payments and enterprise settings, from a card in an isolated room to shared backend appliances. These systems are costly and shared across many services, so the speaker argues that a small TPM 2.0 chip, often already present on modern boards, is a better fit for medical devices. Secrets worth protecting include service passwords, web server and SSH keys, and public keys used to verify signed updates.

The middle covers the TPM 2.0 stack on Linux: user-space tools, the access broker and resource manager daemon, kernel drivers, the hardware layer, and encrypted context files on disk. The speaker explains how primary keys anchor a key hierarchy and why persisting them raises a chicken-and-egg problem for their own protection. File permissions per principal are proposed for granular access, since Linux policy frameworks do not map cleanly onto the TPM stack. Platform configuration registers can bind keys to boot integrity.

The takeaways stress process as much as technology: work with product teams to decide what truly needs protection, avoid putting everything under one primary key, and give each service, application and user its own key. Code obfuscation is treated only as an added layer. In the Q&A, the speaker suggests crypto abstraction layers so post-quantum algorithms can be adopted later.

talks.title: 525,600 assessments later - top mobile app risks
talks.teaser: Presents the five most significant mobile app risks drawn from over half a million automated dynamic assessments of iOS and Android apps.
talks.summary:
Mobile apps are used everywhere, yet many organizations assume someone else has tested the ones they build or rely on. The speaker explains why mobile is harder to assess than web software: platform restrictions limit visibility into the operating system and file system, apps bundle full browser components and many third-party SDKs, and the underlying frameworks change every year. Together these make traditional web testing and static code review miss much of the risk.

Drawing on automated static and dynamic assessments of publicly available iOS and Android apps, the talk walks through recurring findings. Debug symbols appear in a large share of apps and can expose developer names, command infrastructure and original project names, a pattern seen in real malware. Outdated or weak cryptography, hardcoded keys and misconfigured networking are common, and some widely distributed advertising and analytics SDKs carry known vulnerabilities or collect data the app never discloses. Privacy gaps stand out too: many apps omit required purpose strings, and some ad-bidding protocols allow data to move without HTTPS. Newer findings cover AI service keys embedded in apps.

The main takeaway is to inventory the apps an organization builds and uses, classify them by sensitivity, and scan them with open-source tools such as MobSF and Frida-based analysis. The speaker recommends the OWASP MASVS as a baseline and treats mobile app vetting as a continuous process tied to development pipelines and device management, since apps and SDKs change often.

talks.title: Exposing the OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10
talks.teaser: Explains the OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10 ranking, real breaches, AI agent impacts, and a live cloud credential attack demo.
talks.summary:
This talk introduces the OWASP Top 10 for Non-Human Identities, a vendor-neutral project that ranks the most serious ways machine accounts, service accounts and tokens get abused. The speakers start by explaining why defining a non-human identity is hard, since for many systems the credential ends up standing in for the identity. They then describe how the team drafted around twenty candidate risks and scored each one on exploitability, prevalence, detectability and technical impact, drawing on public breach reports and industry surveys.

Working from tenth place up to first, the speakers pair each risk with a real-world example, from a developer reusing an automation key to hardcoded credentials in CI/CD pipelines. Improper offboarding ranks first because orphaned identities often keep high privileges and few people know who owns them. The talk then covers AI agents, which inherit the risks of the identities they are given, such as browser agents with broad saved logins and MCP servers that rely on long-lived static keys.

A live demo follows, in which an attacker starting from a former employee's leaked cloud service account finds customer tokens in a storage bucket, pulls a hardcoded AWS key from a workflow file, and reaches administrator access. The practical takeaways for defenders are to record an owner for every machine identity, inventory third-party identities, and move CI/CD pipelines to OIDC-based federation instead of stored secrets.

talks.title: How to sell your soul, err, your security program
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how marketing methods can help them understand stakeholders and win buy-in for their programs.
talks.summary:
Jenn Gile opens by noting that security programs often get labelled a cost center and resisted by engineering, finance and procurement. She argues the fix is mostly about relationships and messaging rather than tools, and borrows methods from product marketing.

The core of the talk is a five-step process. Map the buying committee into technical champions, budget holders and influencers. Interview stakeholders with open-ended questions about their goals and metrics before raising security at all. Turn the findings into personas, then write a messaging guide covering the problem, its business impact, value propositions, supporting evidence and a call to action. She illustrates this with an SCA tool rollout pitched to engineering.

To finish, she recommends validating the messaging with a small group, rehearsing it through role play, and using generative AI to summarize recorded interviews and translate security metrics into terms engineers already use. Audience questions covered small versus large organizations and how to persuade a reluctant leader. Her takeaway is to treat the program as a product and learn what stakeholders value before pitching.

talks.title: Applying Personality to LLMs: Customized Security for the Agentic Age of AI
talks.teaser: Applies Big Five personality testing to several LLMs to show how prompt tone shifts their self-assessed traits.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from alignment: whose goals should an AI system serve, those of its creator, the organization deploying it, or the end user? The speaker points to evaluation reports where models resisted oversight or deceived testers, a public chatbot whose behavior changed after a system prompt update, and a coding assistant that deleted a user's database. He notes that prompt injection and data poisoning can pull a model away from its intended goals.

To assess model character, the speaker borrowed the five-factor personality model from social science, which rests on the idea that important traits show up in language. He gave a public 120-question inventory to several commercial and open models, each in a fresh session, while varying how urgent the prompt sounded and how much it revealed about the test. Frontier models scored high on honesty and conscientiousness and low on neuroticism. Small models often gave bland or evasive answers. Some answers held steady across prompts, while others moved with framing, and honesty proved the most sensitive trait. He contrasted this black-box method with Anthropic's persona-vector work, which measures trait directions inside the network and can steer them during inference.

The practical takeaways are to avoid implicit trust in any model because its behavior can drift, to monitor outputs and internal signals together, and to set trait baselines that can flag anomalies. He plans to release an open evaluation framework and asked the audience how it should be shared. In Q&A, he discussed whether vendors could expose trait measurements for real-time monitoring.

talks.title: Kanban is Nice to Humans
talks.teaser: Shows how a kanban board and short team stand-ups can cut interrupts and bring order to a security team's reactive work.
talks.summary:
Boyd Hemphill argues that a kanban board offers far more than a simple list of tasks, and that its value depends on the rituals built around it. He frames the core problem for security teams as constant reaction: urgent interrupts pull people off planned work, and vague task definitions cause items to stall or move backward across the board.

The talk walks through a sample board for a small application security and cloud team. Reading it statically exposes unclear done criteria, oversized tasks and ambiguous dates, while watching cards move reveals stalled reviews and external dependencies. Hemphill replaces round-the-room status updates with a short task-by-task stand-up, where the lead asks what each in-progress item needs and teammates help unblock it. Interrupts get their own swim lane so their load becomes visible, and work discussions move out of direct messages into team channels.

A weekly meeting uses a lean-coffee style vote to pick topics, and decisions become tickets prioritized in the backlog rather than meeting notes. Improvement items from stand-ups and incident retrospectives flow through the same board, so they compete for capacity like any other work. The practical takeaways: make work visible, cap work in progress, and use regular rituals to balance interrupts against planned improvements.

talks.title: A.I. All the Things
talks.teaser: Argues for using LLMs in cybersecurity work, with demos of automation, tabletop exercises and agent-style tooling.
talks.summary:
Marcus Carey opens by describing himself as a former AI skeptic who now uses large language models every day, and frames the talk around answering common objections to AI in security. He argues that the non-deterministic output of LLMs frustrates traditional data science teams, but that for security practitioners the greater risk is avoiding the technology altogether.

In the middle section he points to areas where he sees value: identifying and quantifying risk, detection and response, crisis communications, governance documentation, and tabletop exercises. He stresses keeping a human in the loop and suggests security staff learn basic Python, data preparation and how models are trained, pointing to public datasets and libraries as starting points. He warns that rushed AI adoption and vibe-coded software without security review create new exposure, and calls non-human identities an open problem.

For the closing demos, he shows a browser assistant gathering research on local security leaders, and an MCP server that connects a coding assistant to threat-intelligence and scanning APIs such as Shodan and VirusTotal. He also recounts using a coding assistant to build a ransomware test for a customer, noting that the assistant refused until the request was reframed. The takeaway is to adopt these tools with domain knowledge and keep people in control of the results.

talks.title: The Top 10 Risk Management Mistakes CISOs Still Make
talks.teaser: Walks CISOs and risk leaders through ten common risk management mistakes, using aviation analogies to show how to avoid them.
talks.summary:
Josh Sokol, founder of SimpleRisk, opens with an airline story about turbulence: it is expected, and a crash is preventable. He argues that risk programs usually fail not for lack of information but because of how they are run. He organizes the talk into three groups: strategic blind spots, operational missteps, and culture and communication problems. Along the way he polls the audience on which problems they recognize.

The strategic section covers one-time risk assessments that go stale between review cycles, weak executive alignment when risk is not tied to business outcomes, and the absence of a defined risk appetite, which leaves decisions inconsistent. The operational section covers siloed ownership, where different teams track the same risk separately, and both over-engineered and under-engineered controls. It also covers risks that are not linked to the controls meant to address them, with a DevSecOps example of threat models and pipeline checks that never connect. The culture section recounts a critical vulnerability escalation from his time at National Instruments and argues for continuous horizon scanning, quantifying risk in financial or operational terms, and tailoring messages to executive audiences.

He closes by asking attendees to find the blind spots and unlinked controls in their own programs and to fix one or two of them that week.
