In the closing discussion he suggests framing security work around non-security benefits such as faster onboarding and reduced pipeline friction, which he says has produced measurable savings for organizations.

talks.title: Automated Security Testing with OWASP Nettacker
talks.teaser: Shows how the open-source OWASP Nettacker scanner maps networks, finds exposed services and chains scan modules.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces OWASP Nettacker, a free, open-source penetration testing framework written entirely in Python. The speaker opens with recent edge-device vulnerabilities to show how many organisations struggle to inventory the exposed systems they run. Nettacker accepts single addresses, IP ranges, CIDR blocks, domains and URL lists, and can enumerate subdomains first. Its modules cover scanning, vulnerability checks and brute forcing, and several can be chained in one run.

The live demo covered port scans, subdomain discovery and HTTP title and server-version checks. Every result is saved to a built-in database and can be viewed as an HTML report, through a web interface or API, or exported to CSV for inventories. Scan comparison against a baseline flags new hosts, unusual ports, new findings and expiring certificates. Colour coding separates passive checks from modules that send attack payloads or brute-force credentials.

The closing advice is to get permission before scanning any network, because the tool is offensive by design. It installs through Docker or pip and fits into pipelines such as GitHub Actions. Teams can write custom YAML modules, for example to confirm that a pentest finding has been fixed without paying for a retest. The speaker contrasts it with Burp Suite and ZAP, which target one website, and with Nuclei, which needs a URL list.

talks.title: Securing AI-Generated Code in the Development Lifecycle (React Focus)
talks.teaser: Shows how prompt rules and secure React patterns reduce XSS in code written by AI assistants.
talks.summary:
Jim Manico opens with a concern about teams adopting AI coding assistants without security guardrails. He notes that demand for secure coding training is shifting toward AI security, while front-end flaws still appear in generated code because assistants reproduce common insecure patterns from public code.

The middle of the session focuses on React. He lists the risky areas: secrets shipped to the browser, access control enforced only on the client, raw HTML injection, and user-supplied URLs that can carry javascript: payloads. He then asks several chat models to build a user profile page. Most outputs repeated these flaws, and one sanitized the description but still rendered the homepage link unsafely. He then writes a reusable prompt that sets an expert React role, requires sanitization, supplies a URL validation function, and limits third-party dependencies. Rerunning the same request produced clearly better code, though not flawless, and he notes that the grades varied from one model to another.

He closes by recommending that teams keep security requirements in version control, condense them into short rules that models follow reliably, and apply those rules at several points: chat sessions, IDE instructions, and review pipelines. He pairs this with static analysis run by more than one engine. The practical takeaway is that guidance given before code is written can remove many technical bugs earlier and more cheaply than long automated review loops.

talks.title: Why Your Security Metrics Suck, And How to Fix This
talks.teaser: Explains why security metrics often mislead and how to build measures that tell a clear, useful story.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with two confusing charts shared online to show how easily metrics mislead when they lack context. The speaker argues that many security metrics are vague, use loose words like "better" or "easier," skip baselines, and are presented without a clear story. He recalls early work collecting monthly device counts that never explained anything, and points to denominators, such as network segment totals, that people often guess when nobody knows the real number.

The middle of the talk covers what good metrics are for. The speaker describes three purposes: setting a narrative, showing progress against a fixed baseline, and demonstrating cause and effect without falling into the correlation trap. He stresses concrete language, consistent formulas, showing the math, and avoiding feelings or cherry-picked trend lines. He also explains that detail should change by audience, from technical staff to leadership to the board, and contrasts prevention with detection and response. Error rates, staff cuts and budget freezes are offered as examples of measures that can show real business impact.

The close gives a checklist of questions to ask before presenting a metric: what the message is, which variables sit on each axis, whether a non-expert would understand it, whether it is quantitative, and whether the framing gives needed context. The takeaway is that a metric should let an outsider grasp its point without having to be told how to read it.

talks.title: Conquering Castle Envy
talks.teaser: Argues that application security needs production context and a shared model of live systems rather than castle-style fortification.
talks.summary:
Jeff Williams, who wrote the first OWASP Top 10 and the WebGoat training project, opens with a frustration: application security has changed little in about 25 years. He argues the field still leans on a castle model, where teams imagine threats, build defenses, test once and move to operations. Across standards and industry statistics he sees growing backlogs, weak relationships between development and security, and little knowledge of what happens in production.

The middle of the talk compares the application layer to a living city rather than a fortress. He draws a parallel with application performance monitoring, which moved into production because performance problems only appear with real users and data, and suggests security testing needs the same runtime context. He proposes a graph that links business data, assets, infrastructure, software and observed attack activity, fed by sensors at runtime, so threat modeling, penetration testing and compliance can reuse shared information. He also argues that CVSS scores assume the worst, and that many open source libraries in production never load.

The takeaway is to instrument production, prioritize the vulnerabilities attackers are actually targeting and that connect to sensitive assets, and share that context across teams. He works through a budget example in which focusing on the small share of real issues cuts both cost and remediation time sharply.
